title: Laced running stitch
subtitle: A decorative two-colour line formed by threading a second thread in a wave through a running stitch base
excerpt: Laced running stitch works in two passes. A foundation row of running stitches is laid first; a second thread is then laced up and down through the base stitches without piercing the fabric. The result is a wavy, ribbon-like line that can combine two contrasting colours.
sourceNotes: Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), running stitches section (Project Gutenberg #20776). Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882).

glossaryTerms.definition: The thread currently in use that forms the stitches, as distinct from threads already laid or waiting on the back.

content.text: Laced running stitch is a two-pass decorative line stitch. A row of running stitches forms the base, and a second

is laced alternately above and below each base stitch without entering the fabric. The lacing creates a gentle wave or loop pattern along the line. It suits borders on samplers, decorative outlines on clothing and any design where a plain running line needs more character.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton, 2 strands for the running base; 2 strands in a contrasting or toning colour for the lacing

items.label: Needle
items.value: Embroidery needle size 7 or 8 for the base pass; blunt tapestry needle size 24 for the lacing pass

content.text: Secure the base thread on the back and bring it up at point A, at the left end of the line.

Insert the needle down at point B, roughly 4 mm along. Come back up at point C, another 4 mm further on, leaving a gap equal to the stitch length. Continue to the end of the line. Make the stitches and gaps as equal as possible. Fasten off the base thread.
Thread the tapestry needle with the lacing thread and bring it up at the start of the line, just above the first running stitch.
Slide the needle under the first running stitch from below, passing upward through the gap between the stitch and the fabric. Do not pierce the fabric.

Move to the next running stitch and slide the needle under it from above, passing downward. Alternate the direction (below, above, below, above) for each successive stitch. This creates the wave. Keep the lacing thread relaxed so the loops sit evenly.
At the end of the row, take the lacing thread to the back and fasten off.

attrs.heading: When laced running stitch goes wrong

items.symptom: The wave is uneven, with some loops larger than others
items.cause: Unequal tension on the lacing thread as it passes each stitch
items.fix: After passing through each stitch, gently ease the lacing thread to the same height before moving to the next. Even base stitches and gaps help here too.

items.symptom: The lacing thread splits the fabric
items.cause: Using a sharp needle for the lacing pass
items.fix: Use a blunt tapestry needle for lacing. It slips under the base stitches without catching the fabric threads.

content.text: Laced running stitch is used for decorative borders on samplers and clothing, and anywhere a two-colour flowing line is needed. It is closely related to
, which wraps the lacing thread in one direction only for a corded rather than wavy effect. For a similar laced look on a continuous base line,
laces through back stitch and produces a bolder interlocked band.
